searchText: <@!646424665572507648> wanted to highlight this response https://ethresear.ch/t/beacon-chain-light-client-classification/11061/2?u=ralexstokes we actually don't want to introduce this capability for a "light" validator, and i'd say any avenues we find to minimize the validating load should be "upstreamed" into the core consensus protocol where they exist Is it really a good idea to allow attestation from a light client that doesnt necessarily have staked assets at risk? Seems like a potential attack vector especially if the client is really resource-light (easy and cheap to attack using many clients). Levels 1 and 2 make sense to me, but they seem like consecutive stages in a development roadmap rather than a design choice to make at the outset (i.e. develop level 1 light client w client/server model then swap in p2p gossiping later). attestations only make sense in the context of some locked stake (otherwise anyone can go off and attest to whatever valid or invalid chain they desire) the idea of "level 3" is that you are still a bonded validator but you only do the attestation duty assuming you have dropped other data/state necessary to actually produce blocks but this basically makes you a "lazy validator" and for many reasons is not game-theoretically stable wrt a secure consensus protocol 🙂 Ok I see - the l3 light client is a validator with staked eth but reduced validator duties. well more that they just don't do some of them the duties are still there, and/or should be for the "uniformity" reasons i gave in my ethresear.ch response we can actually search for "lazy validator" on ethresear.ch to get a view of the "literature" on this topic, if anyone wants more context and moreover we are trying to mitigate these issues where we can for ethereum validators, e.g. with proofs of custody

excerpts.author: _jmc_.
excerpts.content:
Is it really a good idea to allow attestation from a light client that doesnt necessarily have staked assets at risk? Seems like a potential attack vector especially if the client is really resource-light (easy and cheap to attack using many clients). 

Levels 1 and 2 make sense to me, but they seem like consecutive stages in a development roadmap rather than a design choice to make at the outset (i.e. develop level 1 light client w client/server model then swap in p2p gossiping later).
